title: Which turns about the dot bring each figure back?
description: Three figures with a dot each are tested by turning them about the dot: a plus shape, a line with two small squares, and two long lines joined by a bar. Each figure gets its list of angles of symmetry.
teaching_notes: One idea: test each figure with quarter turns and half turns about its dot and list the turns that fit, the full turn included. Watch for students who count the parts of a figure instead of testing the turns.

source: Figure it Out Q1 (section 9.2, first block)
video_script.why: The child lists the angles of symmetry of three figures by turning each one about its dot, the same way a square was tested in a quarter turn.
video_script.substitution: Trace each figure, pin the dot and turn the tracing to see which turns land it exactly on the original.
video_script.anchor: three figures with a dot each: the plus shape of two equal rectangles, a vertical line with a small square on the right of each end, and two long vertical lines joined by a short bar
video_script.payoff_line: The three figures have four, one and two angles of symmetry

final_answer.value: a) 90, 180, 270 and 360 degrees; b) 360 degrees only; c) 180 and 360 degrees
final_answer.spoken: the plus fits after four turns, the line with squares only after the full turn, and the third figure after the half turn and the full turn

maths_rules: A turn about the dot after which a figure looks exactly the same is called an angle of symmetry; the full turn of 360 degrees always fits
Figure a: the plus of 2 equal rectangles has 4 equal arms, 90 degrees apart; each quarter turn puts an arm on the next arm, so 90, 180, 270 and 360 degrees all fit

Figure b: a vertical line with a small square on the right of each end; a 180 degree turn puts the top square on the left of the bottom end, where there is no square, so it does not fit; 90 and 270 degrees lay the line flat, so they do not fit; only 360 degrees fits

Figure c: 2 long vertical lines joined by a short horizontal bar through their middles; a 180 degree turn swaps the two long lines and they match; 90 and 270 degrees lay the long lines flat, so they do not fit; 180 and 360 degrees fit
Counts of angles of symmetry: figure a 4, figure b 1, figure c 2, each including 360 degrees
video_script.design: One idea: test each figure with quarter and half turns about its dot and list the turns that fit. Assumes the child has turned a square by quarter turns. Wrong idea: the number of parts gives the number of turns. The three figures stay on the board all video.

narration: <bookmark mark='term'/>Turn a figure about its dot. If it looks exactly the same afterwards, that turn is called an angle of symmetry.
<bookmark mark='full'/>The full turn of three hundred and sixty degrees always fits.
<bookmark mark='card'/>Try a plain rectangle card, pinned at its middle. A quarter turn stands it upright, so it does not fit.
<bookmark mark='halfcard'/>A half turn swaps its ends, and it fits.
